name: @jexs/mcp

tools.name: search_ops
tools.description: Find Jexs operations by name or description. Start here: there are hundreds of ops, and this returns only the matching ones with their package, owning Node class and return type. Follow up with describe_op for the full signature.

query.description: Text to look for in operation names and descriptions, e.g. "sort", "http", "base64".

package.description: Optional. Restrict to one package, e.g. "@jexs/server".

tools.name: describe_op
tools.description: Show the full signature of a Jexs operation: owning Node class and package, description, return type, sibling keys (with which are required and which belong to a specific operation), variant operations, and examples. Also accepts a global step key (as, return, catch, then, bubble).

op.description: Operation key, e.g. "if", "foreach", "directory", or a global step key like "then".

tools.name: list_nodes
tools.description: List every registered Jexs Node class and its operation keys (variant ops shown inline), plus the global step keys. Large: prefer search_ops unless you want the whole surface.

package.description: Optional. Only list Node classes from this package, e.g. "@jexs/client".

tools.name: describe_def
tools.description: Show a $defs shape contributed by a node (e.g. "_routeNode"). Accepts a bare name or a #/$defs/<name> ref.

tools.name: validate_file
tools.description: Validate a Jexs JSON file against the project's generated schema (the same one the editor uses) and report where it fails. Use this to check a template you just wrote.

filePath.description: Path to the JSON file, relative to the resolver root.

tools.name: inspect_file
tools.description: Read a Jexs JSON file and report which node operation keys it uses, any keys that look like typos, and advisory lint about dispatch foot-guns.

filePath.description: Path to the JSON file, relative to the resolver root.

tools.name: resolve_expression
tools.description: Resolve a Jexs JSON expression through the live resolver and return the result. Pass the expression as JSON (object/array/value), not a string. It runs against a real server resolver with full node access, so it can read files, hit the network and touch the database exactly as the app would.

expression.description: A Jexs JSON expression to resolve, e.g. { "$concat": ["a", "b"] }.

vars.description: Optional. Context variables to seed, so the expression can read them via { "$var": "name" }. Taken as-is: values are not resolved, so a var may hold steps or other templates. To compute a value, do it inside the expression (e.g. a leading $setVars step).

instructions:
Jexs is a JSON expression language: a step is an object whose one `$`-prefixed key names the op it runs (`{ "$concat": [...] }`), and its other keys are that op's options. An object without a `$` key is plain data. A JSON array is a step sequence; the last step's value is the result.

Reads come from context via `{ "$var": "name" }`; writes go through `$as` or `$setVars`. There is no get/set node.

Use these tools instead of guessing at key names: `search_ops` to find an operation, `describe_op` for its siblings and return type, `describe_def` for a `#/$defs/` shape a node contributes, `inspect_file` and `validate_file` to check a template you wrote, and `resolve_expression` to actually run one.
